readerTitle: Which fridge does your juice go in?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 착즙 주스 제조사, 사무실 청소 업체) · 수치 없음, 모든 상황은 설명용
insight: 포지셔닝은 '무엇이 좋은가'보다 먼저 '누구와 비교될 것인가'를 정하는 일이다. 비교 대상이 정해져야 어떤 차별점이 통하는지도 정해진다.
misconception: 좋은 제품이면 장점을 많이 늘어놓을수록 잘 팔린다. 같은 업계 경쟁사만 경쟁 상대다.

sources.text: Keller, K. L., Sternthal, B., & Tybout, A. M. (2002). Three Questions You Need to Ask About Your Brand. Harvard Business Review. (준거 틀, 동등점·차별점 개념)

factChecks.note: 모든 인물과 회사(Ana의 주스, Bea의 청소 업체)는 가상입니다. 통계나 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.
6번 카드의 '착즙 주스는 며칠, 에너지 음료는 수개월 상온 보관'은 일반적인 설명입니다. 고압살균(HPP) 처리 주스는 유통기한이 더 길 수 있으므로 'days, not months'라는 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
4번 카드 선택지의 'superfoods'와 건강 관련 문구는 국가별 표시·광고 규제 대상일 수 있습니다. 레슨은 법률 조언을 하지 않으며, 피드백에서 일반적인 위험으로만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: Which fridge does your juice go in?
body: Ana makes cold-pressed juice in a small rented kitchen. Local cafés love it. Now a regional grocery chain offers her a trial in 20 stores.
The buyer has one question before anything else: *"Which fridge do you want to be in?"* It sounds like a shelving detail. It decides who her rivals will be.

image.label: One juice bottle facing three different store fridges
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 라벨 없는 주스 병 하나가 가운데 서 있고, 뒤로 냉장고 세 개: 주스 냉장고, 계산대 옆 에너지 음료·아이스커피 냉장고, 건강식품 코너 진열대. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should Ana's juice compete?
body: Same bottle, same recipe, same price. The buyer can place it in one of three spots. Which would you pick?

options.text: The juice fridge, next to other cold-pressed brands
options.feedback: Shoppers instantly know what it is. But Ana becomes one of many green bottles, judged mostly on price and brand name. That's the **frame of reference** at work.

options.text: The grab-and-go fridge by the till, as an afternoon pick-me-up
options.feedback: Now her rivals are iced coffee and energy drinks, and the bottle looks unusual among them. She gains a fresh story but must prove she belongs in that fridge.

options.text: The health aisle, as a daily wellness habit
options.feedback: A loyal, higher-paying shopper. But that aisle invites health promises she may not be able to back up, and shoppers there expect proof.

choice.afterReveal: There's no single right fridge. Each one picks a different set of rivals and a different question in the shopper's mind.

cards.title: The frame picks your rivals.
body: A **frame of reference** is the group of alternatives customers compare you to. You don't just choose a shelf. You choose the question shoppers ask.

In the juice fridge, they ask: *"Which juice is best?"* By the till, they ask: *"What gets me through the afternoon?"* Ana picks the second. Her rivals are now coffee and energy drinks, not other juices.

image.label: Same bottle, three frames, three different rivals
image.brief: 가로 3단 인포그래픽. 같은 주스 병 아래 각각 "Juice fridge → other juices", "By the till → coffee, energy drinks", "Health aisle → supplements". 가운데 칸을 강조 색으로 표시. 로고 없음.

cards.title: What should the label lead with?
body: Ana's juice now sits between iced coffee and energy drinks. She has room for one big line on the front of the bottle.

options.feedback: True and appealing, but it's what every juice says. Next to an energy drink, it doesn't explain why to switch. A strong claim in the wrong frame.

options.text: "Real fruit. No caffeine. No 4 p.m. crash."
options.feedback: This is a **point of difference** that matters inside the chosen frame. It answers the shopper's question better than coffee does.
A list, not a reason. It also edges toward health claims that need proof and may be regulated where she sells.

cards.title: Different where it counts, equal where it must.
body: A **point of difference** is a reason to choose you over the other options in your frame. It only works if customers in that frame care about it.

Ana also needs **points of parity**: the basics she must match so shoppers accept her as a real option. Here that means a bottle you can drink on the go, a spot near the till, and a price not far from an iced coffee.
Organic stays on the back label. It's nice, not the reason to buy.

cards.title: Every frame brings its own rules.
body: Energy drinks can sit at room temperature for months. Fresh juice needs a fridge and lasts days, not months.

If the store won't give Ana fridge space by the till, or her deliveries can't restock often enough to avoid empty shelves and waste, the clever frame falls apart. A frame is only useful if your operation can serve it every day.

image.label: Small refrigerated van making frequent store deliveries
image.brief: 작은 냉장 밴이 매장 세 곳을 잇는 짧은 루트를 반복해서 도는 지도 일러스트. 시계 아이콘으로 잦은 배송을 표현. 차량과 매장에 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's an office cleaning company.
body: Bea runs a commercial cleaning company. A growing 40-person office isn't comparing her with other cleaning firms. It's deciding whether to hire its own cleaner instead.

options.text: "The lowest hourly rate in the city"
options.feedback: This argues inside the wrong frame. Against an in-house hire, price per hour isn't the question, and she starts a race she may not win.

options.text: "Like your own cleaner, without the gaps. If someone is ill, we send cover the same day."
options.feedback: She accepts the real **frame of reference** (hiring in-house) and leads with a **point of difference** that matters there: no missed days.
A real plus, but an in-house cleaner could use the same products. It isn't what the office is deciding on.

cards.title: Choose who you're compared with, then win on what matters there.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Frame of reference:** pick the alternatives customers will compare you to. **Points of difference:** lead with what wins inside that frame, and match the basics everyone expects.
**Try it today:** write down what your customers would buy if you didn't exist. Then write the one reason they'd choose you over it.
cards.softwareNote: A small analytics tool framed as "a cheaper dashboard app" gets compared on features and price. Framed as "a replacement for the weekly spreadsheet report," it's judged on time saved, and the point of difference becomes obvious.
